The manuscript reports a bistable origami-based passive thermal switch achieving an exceptionally high thermal switching ratio. The system exploits a snap-through instability between two distinct mechanical states, enhancing the difference in thermal contact. switches. The current manuscript primarily adapts this well-known concept to a thermal
regulation context without introducing substantial mechanistic or material-level innovation.

novelty of our work. By thoroughly searching academic databases, we did not find any similar
previous work as the reviewer indicated. Thus, we would like to ask the reviewer to point out
the exact literature that has reported using a bistable origami structure for thermal switching,
so that we can compare or cite. We acknowledge that bistable origami and snap-through
structures have been widely utilized for other areas, but it is not fair to conclude that everything
following such mechanical design is not novel.

reporting a bistable origami thermal switch. We have collected most related papers that we can
found to compare with our work, as shown in the table below. Current thermal switches
typically depend on external fields, rely on slow phase-change processes, or fail to provide a
strong binary response. Our approach addresses all of these limitations and attains a record
switching ratio across all reported thermal switch designs.

attempts of using SMA for thermal switching have only achieved best switching ratio of

leaks through the SMA wires when the switch is toggled OFF. In addition, the bistability

mechanistic innovation, beyond simply adding SMA to bistable origami. It may be easy

### Reviewer 1

The manuscript presents an interesting design for ultra-high ratio passive thermal switching based on a bistable origami metastructure. The key contribution lies in achieving a record thermal switching ratio (13,984 in vacuum and 1,360 in air) through a purely passive, energy-free mechanism. By integrating the snap-through bistability of an origami structure with the temperature-responsive behavior of shape memory alloys and elastic springs, the authors have introduced a novel architecture capable of reversible, autonomous, and energy-efficient thermal regulation. The idea is quite original and validated through experiments. The various demonstrations show its potential for real-world impact. The manuscript is generally well-written and easy to follow. With further clarifications and broader contextual discussion, it would make an excellent contribution to the field.
I have the following questions to the authors:
1.The origami structure is interesting. However, I wonder how reproducible is the switching temperature across different fabrication batches, given the manual assembly and sensitivity to crease geometry? What is the success rate during experiments?
2.Can the authors comment on the possible miniaturization limits of the origami metastructure—how small could such switches be made while retaining functionality? This design would be very useful if it can be put on advanced chips.
3.If the origami base is made with materials other than the polymide film, would the design still maintain high switching ratio? Some theoretical or numerical analysis on this material-dependency is suggested.
4.The manuscript mentions ~10 s response time. Can the authors provide an analysis of the switching kinetics—what limits the response (SMA heating/cooling, mechanical inertia, or contact formation)? Could the switching speed be enhanced (e.g., by thinner SMA wires, or reduced thermal mass)?
5.Page 4: “The origami pattern of the BOS is illustrated in Fig. 1c, which composes of five axisymmetric arms…” The verb “composes of” should be “is composed of.”
6.Be consistent with figure references: sometimes written as “Fig. 1b” and elsewhere as “Figure 1b.”
7.Ensure consistent units (W m⁻² K⁻¹ vs W/m²K) and correct symbols for temperature differences.
8.Page 6: “The ultra-high switching ratio originates of the bistable origami switch.” The word after “originates” should be “from” instead of “of.”
9.Include scale bars in all optical/IR images (Figs. 1e, 2b, 4b).

### Reviewer 2

The manuscript reports a bistable origami-based passive thermal switch achieving an exceptionally high thermal switching ratio. The system exploits a snap-through instability between two distinct mechanical states, enhancing the difference in thermal contact. Passive actuation is realized by integrating shape-memory alloy actuators at the hinge regions, while a TPU elastic wire introduces pre-strain to ensure reversible ON/OFF switching. The concept demonstrates an elegant combination of structural mechanics and thermal actuation, potentially valuable for autonomous thermal management.
While the overall framework is interesting and the fabrication appears well executed, I believe the novelty and clarity of the work are somewhat limited for a high-impact journal. Bistable origami structures and snap-through–based mechanisms have been widely utilized in various mechanical and functional systems, including actuators, reconfigurable devices, and thermal switches. The current manuscript primarily adapts this well-known concept to a thermal regulation context without introducing substantial mechanistic or material-level innovation.
Furthermore, many details—particularly regarding the actuator design, dynamic operation, and local stress behavior—are confined to the Supplementary Information and only briefly summarized in the main text. The work would benefit from clearer visualization, quantitative actuation analysis, and expanded discussion of physical limits and applications. For these reasons, I would recommend “Reject or Reject and Resubmit after Major Revision.”
Below are my questions and suggestions to improve paper.
1. The structure is not clearly visible. Please provide close-up images of important regions.
2. The sequential deformation process should be better illustrated in the main text. Using a high-speed camera or slow-motion video would help visualize the snap-through transition.
3. Although the limitation comes from the temperature-based actuation, the switching speed appears slow. What happens if the heating and cooling rates are increased?
4. Although the authors varied the folding angles and arm lengths, the design is still limited to a five-fold symmetric (pentagonal) structure. It would be desirable to demonstrate the same concept in other geometries or configurations.
4-1. The current design has five arms. Is it possible to design with fewer or more arms?
4-2. If the arm lengths differ, would the top plate tilt relative to the ground, creating an inclined surface?
5. What happens if only part of the SMA actuators are heated instead of all of them?
6. Many results are only summarized in the manuscript just as ‘Supplementary Notes’. Each Supplementary Figure should be described or cited in the text with corresponding explanations.
7. The simulation is too macroscopic. More detailed modeling of the hinge regions or local stress distribution is needed. Are the forces acting only on the legs?
8. What is the maximum load that the BOS top plate can support while still maintaining functional snap-through switching?

mechanistic innovation, beyond simply adding SMA to bistable origami. It may be easy

mechanically bistable as traditionally defined --- it becomes bistable as a system under

the repeatable thermal regulation cycles without external sensing and actuation.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

The manuscript presents an interesting design for ultra-high ratio passive thermal switching based on a bistable origami metastructure. The key contribution lies in achieving a record thermal switching ratio (13,984 in vacuum and 1,360 in air) through a purely passive, energy-free mechanism. By integrating the snap-through bistability of an origami structure with the temperature-responsive behavior of shape memory alloys and elastic springs, the authors have introduced a novel architecture capable of reversible, autonomous, and energy-efficient thermal regulation. ### Reviewer 2

The manuscript reports a bistable origami-based passive thermal switch achieving an exceptionally high thermal switching ratio. The system exploits a snap-through instability between two distinct mechanical states, enhancing the difference in thermal contact. Passive actuation is realized by integrating shape-memory alloy actuators at the hinge regions, while a TPU elastic wire introduces pre-strain to ensure reversible ON/OFF switching. The concept demonstrates an elegant combination of structural mechanics and thermal actuation, potentially valuable for autonomous thermal management.
While the overall framework is interesting and the fabrication appears well executed, I believe the novelty and clarity of the work are somewhat limited for a high-impact journal. Bistable origami structures and snap-through–based mechanisms have been widely utilized in various mechanical and functional systems, including actuators, reconfigurable devices, and thermal switches. The current manuscript primarily adapts this well-known concept to a thermal regulation context without introducing substantial mechanistic or material-level innovation.
Furthermore, many details—particularly regarding the actuator design, dynamic operation, and local stress behavior—are confined to the Supplementary Information and only briefly summarized in the main text. The work would benefit from clearer visualization, quantitative actuation analysis, and expanded discussion of physical limits and applications. For these reasons, I would recommend “Reject or Reject and Resubmit after Major Revision.”
Below are my questions and suggestions to improve paper.
1. The structure is not clearly visible. Please provide close-up images of important regions.
2. The sequential deformation process should be better illustrated in the main text. Using a high-speed camera or slow-motion video would help visualize the snap-through transition.
3. Although the limitation comes from the temperature-based actuation, the switching speed appears slow. What happens if the heating and cooling rates are increased?
4. Although the authors varied the folding angles and arm lengths, the design is still limited to a five-fold symmetric (pentagonal) structure. It would be desirable to demonstrate the same concept in other geometries or configurations.
4-1. The current design has five arms. Is it possible to design with fewer or more arms?
4-2. If the arm lengths differ, would the top plate tilt relative to the ground, creating an inclined surface?
5. What happens if only part of the SMA actuators are heated instead of all of them?
6. Many results are only summarized in the manuscript just as ‘Supplementary Notes’. Each Supplementary Figure should be described or cited in the text with corresponding explanations.
7. The simulation is too macroscopic. More detailed modeling of the hinge regions or local stress distribution is needed. Are the forces acting only on the legs?
8. What is the maximum load that the BOS top plate can support while still maintaining functional snap-through switching?

The manuscript reports a bistable origami-based passive thermal switch achieving an
exceptionally high thermal switching ratio. The system exploits a snap-through instability
between two distinct mechanical states, enhancing the difference in thermal contact. Passive
actuation is realized by integrating shape-memory alloy actuators at the hinge regions, while a
TPU elastic wire introduces pre-strain to ensure reversible ON/OFF switching. The concept
demonstrates an elegant combination of structural mechanics and thermal actuation, potentially
valuable for autonomous thermal management.
Response: We thank the Reviewer for the positive comments about our work. We especially
thank the reviewer for recognizing the “elegant combination of structural mechanics and
thermal actuation” in our work. Indeed, simply adding SMA wires to a bistable origami
structure would not produce the same thermal switching functionality. Therefore, the core
innovation of our work is the proposed design that “elegantly” orchestrate smart materials and
smart structures to enable a repeatable, high-performance, passive thermal switch.
While the overall framework is interesting and the fabrication appears well executed, I believe
the novelty and clarity of the work are somewhat limited for a high-impact journal. Bistable
origami structures and snap-through–based mechanisms have been widely utilized in various
mechanical and functional systems, including actuators, reconfigurable devices, and thermal
switches. The current manuscript primarily adapts this well-known concept to a thermal
regulation context without introducing substantial mechanistic or material-level innovation.
Response: We are sorry that our previous submission did not impress the reviewer for its
novelty. However, we must respectfully disagree with the reviewer’s statement about the
novelty of our work. By thoroughly searching academic databases, we did not find any similar
previous work as the reviewer indicated. Thus, we would like to ask the reviewer to point out
the exact literature that has reported using a bistable origami structure for thermal switching,
so that we can compare or cite. We acknowledge that bistable origami and snap-through
structures have been widely utilized for other areas, but it is not fair to conclude that everything
following such mechanical design is not novel.
Regarding thermal switches, to the best of our knowledge, we have not found any paper
reporting a bistable origami thermal switch. We have collected most related papers that we can
found to compare with our work, as shown in the table below. Current thermal switches
typically depend on external fields, rely on slow phase-change processes, or fail to provide a
strong binary response. Our approach addresses all of these limitations and attains a record
switching ratio across all reported thermal switch designs.
It may be helpful for us to reiterate the novel contribution of our work.
(1) To the best of our knowledge, we are the first work to report a mechanical thermal switch
using bistable origami structure with record-high switching ratio. In previous research,
attempts of using SMA for thermal switching have only achieved best switching ratio of
2070 (Ref [15], nature energy, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41560-018-0243-8), owing the fact
that SMA itself is of high thermal conductivity. Using the proposed bistable origami design,
we are able separate the SMA from the device and the heat sink, such that no heat flow
leaks through the SMA wires when the switch is toggled OFF. In addition, the bistability
of the BOS helps to maintain a steady thermal conductivity whenever the switch is ON or
OFF, achieving clear binary effect.
(2) The repeatable passive thermal regulation cycle that we reported represents substantial
mechanistic innovation, beyond simply adding SMA to bistable origami. It may be easy
to push a bistable structure from its original state to the other state, however, it is extremely
difficult to bring it back to the original states without external help. In this work, we
achieved this by carefully optimizing the combined forces of the bistable origami, the SMA
wire, the rotational springs, and elastic regulators. As shown in Fig. 3, when the temperature
of the device rises to the designated degree, the actuation force of SMA wires suppresses
the resistant forces from the elastic components and pushes the BOS down (turning ON).
In this state, the thermal load is critical for maintaining the driving force of the SMA wires.
Without the thermal load, the BOS cannot stay at this state, and it will automatically spring
back to its original state (turning OFF). Therefore, the complete BOS is no longer
mechanically bistable as traditionally defined --- it becomes bistable as a system under
the thermal load. By simply adding SMA to the bistable origami, it is impossible to achieve
the repeatable thermal regulation cycles without external sensing and actuation.
